Student Growth: Introductory Concepts
• The concept of student growth isn’t as difficult to understand and popular perception
suggests.
• Calculations may be complicated but knowing how to calculate student growth is not
synonymous with understanding student growth:
• The number π (pi=3.14159…) is difficult to calculate but is simple to understand
conceptually.
• Height and weight percentiles associated with children are difficult to calculate but
are simple to understand conceptually.
• Computational details are important but often obscure a simple conceptual basis.

Student Growth: Introductory Concepts
• There are 3 general approaches of calculating student growth:
• Growth as an amount of change (i.e., gain).
• Growth as a norm/peer referenced quantity.
• Growth as a criterion referenced quantity.

Student Growth: Introductory Concepts
• Growth as an amount of change:
• What could be more simple?
• Like height or weight just calculate the amount of change.
• Requires a vertical scale (which Hawaii has with SBA)
• Growth = Score Time 2 - Score Time 1
• Not as simple as it seems:
• Comparisons between students often leads to wrong conclusions
• Interpreting change requires context.

• Just as an inch isn’t necessarily an inch; a scale score point isn’t necessarily a scale score point.
• The point here is that many people who know something about psychometrics will say that
“uneven gains” is due to education measurement scales not having strict measurement properties.

Student Growth: Introductory Concepts
• This is analogous to height/weight measures for infants.
• Growth (i.e., change) amounts are tricky to interpret and require context.
• Peer based comparisons used by growth analyses are a way to acquire that context.
• Regression is the statistical technique to mathematically model these peer based
comparisons.

An infant male toddler is measured at 2 and 3 years of age and is shown to have
grown 4 inches. The magnitude of increase—4 inches—is a well understood quantity
that any parent can grasp and calculate at home using a simple yardstick. However,
parents leaving their pediatrician’s office knowing only how much their child has
grown would likely be wanting for more information: Parents are not interested in an
absolute magnitude of growth, but instead in a norm-referenced quantity locating
that 4 inch increase alongside the height increases of similar children.

Student Growth: Introductory Concepts
• Peer-based analyses are also called norm-referenced analyses.
• Like with infant height/weight charts, peers are children/student with similar
characteristics.
• For growth analyses using large scale assessments, peers are students with (at
least) the same scale score history on the same tests.
• Peer based norms are invaluable in providing context for stakeholders to
understand student growth.
• The Hawaii SGP Model creates growth norms for all students using regression (i.e.,
peer-based) analyses.
• These norms allow stakeholders to understand what an ambitious yet reasonable
expectation is for each student.

Student Growth Percentiles
• Research on the SGP model began in 2007.
• Based upon work in Colorado, the norm-referenced model was
extended to include a criterion-referenced component.
• Work in other states incorporating the model into state reporting
and accountability systems occurred in subsequent years and
student growth became more common across state assessment
systems.
• Goal or the model is to create an individual level growth metric
that is informative to different stakeholders ranging from parents
to policy makers.

History of student growth in Hawaii
• Begun in 2012 as part of Hawaii’s successful RttT grant.
• Originally focused on teacher evaluation.
• Included use of interactive visualizations to help communicate SGP results.
• Included the calculation of student growth percentiles (SGPs) and student growth
targets (SGTs) (not sure whether SGTs were used).
• Used (and not used) in different ways over the last decade.
• Used to investigate COVID-19 related academic impact and recovery.

SGP Output
• An SGP is a student level result that can be aggregated across any groups of interest.
• The goal was to help everyone see that the “performance of the system” is based upon the
performance of individual students. And if we want to make the system perform better then
we need to help students perform better and this is what better performance means
(higher rates of learning)
• As I mentioned, early on the interest was looking at classroom (i.e., instructor) level growth.
• This summary aggregation is akin to value-added metrics (I would argue that value-added in
an inference as opposed to a statistic itself).
• The goals of SGP were always to be first and foremost a descriptive measurement student
growth learning.
• As part of that communication effort, individual student reports were produced for all
students in the state 5 to 10 years ago.

SGP Output
• Those of you who have heard me talk about COVID-19 impact analyses have heard me discuss at
length the difference between examining status (e.g., percent proficient changes over time)
versus looking at growth (e.g., median baseline SGP) over time.
• The pandemic’s impact on student achievement taught me some invaluable lessons regarding
how results are understood and communicated, especially to non-technical stakeholders.
• In particular:
• Status/Attainment is akin to a point in time measurement of what students know and can
do.
• Growth/Learning is taking to velocity - the change in status/attainment over time.
• The pandemic disrupted the conditions of learning which in turn slowed learning down which led
to lower attainment.
• When we examine growth results think of this as the (average) velocity of learning.

SGP & Policy
• Over the last couple of years as states reset long-term trends due to the impact of the
COVID-19 pandemic I’ve seen too many bad interpretations of trend data.
• The implicit goal behind reporting percent proficient trend data is to hopefully seeing
increasing rates of proficiency over time (we want more kids to be proficient in ELA and
math).
• Increases, if they exist, are often modest.
• Though percent proficient is critically important, I would argue that it is an impoverished
and incoherent way to motivate the changes that we actually believe we have some
control over.
• Achievement/attainment are an outcome of growth/learning. It is the latter that we have
some control over, yet we focus the attention of educators on the former.
